candidates.draft_body:

'And every one that is born, the flesh of whose foreskin is not circumcised on the eighth day, belongs not to the children of the covenant which the Lord made with Abraham, but to the children of destruction; nor is there moreover any sign on him that he is the Lord's, but (he is destined) to be destroyed and slain from the earth' — Jubilees' severe formulation of the circumcision-covenant. Tewahedo practice retains circumcision on the 8th day for boys as cultural continuity (not soteriological necessity in the Christian dispensation, but unbroken Abrahamic-covenant continuity).

candidates.draft_body:

'And the uncircumcised male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin on the eighth day, that soul shall be cut off from his people, for he has broken My covenant' — Jubilees doubles the Genesis-17 mandate, specifying the eighth-day timing with covenantal severity. Tewahedo Christian circumcision (gəzrät) preserved on the eighth day — uniquely among major Christian communions — draws canonical warrant directly from this verse. The Tewahedo holds that circumcision is not abrogated by baptism (the standard Western and Eastern Orthodox view) but transformed: the Christian receives BOTH circumcision (as patriarchal sign of belonging) and baptism (as new-covenant rebirth), without conflating them.

candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'For the law of this ordinance is for all generations forever, that there is no circumcising of the days, and no omitting of one day out of the eight days' — Jubilees frames the eighth-day timing as permanently fixed, with no liturgical flexibility. The Tewahedo continues the eighth-day practice with this exact non-negotiability: a Christian male child whose parents delay circumcision past the eighth day must seek priestly counsel; the rite is not abolished by Christ but kept as a sign that the Tewahedo are children of Abraham in the patriarchal-fleshly as well as the new-covenant-spiritual sense. This is one of the Tewahedo's distinctive theological-anthropological positions vis-à-vis the rest of Christendom.

'For the nature of all the angels of the presence and all the angels of sanctification has been so from the day of their creation, and before the angels of the presence and the angels of sanctification He hath sanctified Israel, that they should be with Him and with His holy angels' — Jubilees makes the astonishing claim that the highest angels are themselves circumcised (15:27). Tewahedo angelology preserves this: the seraphim and cherubim are imaged in iconographic tradition with the patriarchal sign, anchoring the Tewahedo conviction that circumcision is heavenly-cosmic in scope, not merely Mosaic-national. The mid-2nd-c. Jubilees here resolves the apparent paradox of an ostensibly bodily sign being also a heavenly mark: the highest angels were created bearing it.

candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And there will be great wrath from the Lord against the children of Israel, because they have forsaken His covenant and have turned away from His word' — Jubilees prophesies Israel's future apostasy on the very day God establishes the circumcision covenant. The pattern (covenant-cut + foreseen-apostasy + remnant-preservation) is the canonical shape Tewahedo historiography reads in its own history: each great covenant moment (Frumentius's 4th-c. evangelization, Yared's 6th-c. liturgical codification, Yäkuno Amlak's 13th-c. dynasty-restoration, Twahǝdo-Kalcedonia 451-1959 stand) is followed by partial apostasy and remnant preservation. The remnant pattern is canonical, not accidental.
